newsitem.title: VENEZUELA: Troubled Venezuelan airline Viasa suspends flights.
newsitem.headline: Troubled Venezuelan airline Viasa suspends flights.

text.p: Troubled Venezuelan airline Viasa grounded all its planes on Thursday for at least two weeks as it teetered on the brink of bankruptcy.
"Due to the company's condition, operations have been suspended as of today (at 4 p.m. local time, (2000 GMT))" the company's executive board said in a statement.

The suspension was effective until at least Feb. 8, when an extraordinary shareholders' meeting will decide "whether we increase the company's capital or declare it bankrupt," Victor Sanchez, executive secretary of the board, told reporters.
The long-standing woes of Venezuela's flag carrier airline took a turn for the worse earlier this month when workers overwhelmingly rejected an emergency cost-cutting plan.
Viasa, whose majority shareholder is Spanish national airline Iberia, registered a loss of $30 million last year and has not made a profit since Iberia took over management in 1991.

The president of Viasa's labour union, William Bracho, urged employees to remain calm and said he hoped an agreement could be reached in the next few days between the Venezuelan and Spanish governments to allow Viasa planes to fly again.
"We hope that this suspension, which I disagree with, doesn't mean the end of the company," he told reporters.
The announcement of the flights' suspension came in a note sent to ground staff at Simon Bolivar International Airport, at Maiquetia, outside Caracas.
The company operates 10 flights daily, including to Madrid, London, Buenos Aires, Lima, Bogota and Quito.
Iberia, which holds 45 percent of Viasa, says it has already injected $272 million into the loss-making airline and cannot provide more financing under European Union directives.
Iberia Planning Director Javier Alvarez "deeply" deplored the flights' suspension and said "a bankruptcy cannot suit Iberia because it would mean a loss of $272 million."
The Venezuelan government, with a 40 percent stake in the airline, has also repeatedly refused to pump more money into the airline, which has 2,200 employees.

Some government officials have put the blame for Viasa's misfortunes on Iberia. Ministers have admitted a bankruptcy would deal a strong blow to Venezuela's foreign image as the country emerges from three years of economic crisis.
Venezuela's largest bank, banco Provincial, holds the remaining 15 percent share of Viasa.
